newsitem.title: USA: ABC says news gathering may need new strategies.
newsitem.headline: ABC says news gathering may need new strategies.

text.p: The president of the Walt Disney Co ABC television network unit's news division said unless ABC's lawsuit loss to supermarket chain Food Lion Inc were overturned on appeal, journalists would have to rethink newsgathering techniques.
Roone Arledge took issue with a federal jury's award of $5.5 million in punitive damages to Food Lion during a special edition of the "Nightline" program late Wednesday.

"If the verdict stands, all journalists are going to have to find a different way to do these things," Arledge said of the hidden camera investigation of food handling practices at the grocery chain by the "PrimeTime Live" program.

Salisbury, North Carolina-based Food Lion sued New York- based ABC over a 1992 "PrimeTime Live" report that charged Food Lion sold spoiled meat and other outdated merchandise and did not use sanitary food handling practices.

The jury found late last year that ABC committed fraud, trespass, and breach of loyalty when two of its producers obtained jobs at Food Lion stores -- one as a meat handler and the other as a deli clerk. The panel awarded Food Lion compensatory damages of $1,400.

The producers worked undercover with cameras hidden in their hair and recorders under their smocks. They filmed spoiling deli products, meat cutters and machines that were not properly cleaned and other unsanitary conditions for the Nov. 5, 1992, broadcast in a "ratings sweeps" period.

During Wednesday's 90-minute live broadcast of "Nightline" in a Wake Forest University chapel here, two women in the audience had cameras hidden in their purses and demonstrated how easy it was to film with the device.
Arledge defended the use of hidden cameras and said several lawyers and news executives are consulted before the cameras, often as tiny as a tube of lipstick, are used.
"It has to pass a very rigid, in-house set of rules," he said.

He was joined in a panel discussion on the industry's assessment of itself with jurors who decided the case, "PrimeTime Live" co-anchor Diane Sawyer, Executive Producer Don Hewitt of the "60 Minutes" newsmagazine program of Westinghouse Electric Corp's CBS television network, former Sen. Alan Simpson, Food Lion representatives and a university professor.
"The American people do not like hidden cameras; they do not like deception," said Simpson.

Jury foreman Gregory Mack said the verdict hinged on the ABC producers falsifying the applications for jobs at the grocer. He said that proved consciousness of wrongdoing, a key issue in the case under the judge's instruction.
